samples.summary: The new `yorkie-service` identity is an unscoped, unrevocable master credential: `decide()` returns ALLOW for it on every document key, every verb and every method, and the token is transmitted off-process to the Yorkie server on every RPC
samples.evidence:
`decide()` short-circuits to `ALLOW` for any token whose `typ` is `yorkie-service` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215-217) — before the document-key parse, before the verb check, before `REVISION_READ_METHODS`. The credential is therefore equivalent to "read+write+full revision history on every document in the project", with no binding to a document, a method, or a client.

The justification given for accepting that blast radius is that the token "never leaves the process" (yorkie-service-token.ts:23, repeated in docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:131 and packages/backend/README.md:519). That is not true, and cannot be: the token is handed to the Yorkie SDK's `authTokenInjector` (yorkie.service.ts:74) precisely so the SDK sends it to `YORKIE_RPC_ADDR` on every RPC and Yorkie echoes it back in the webhook body. So the token crosses the network to a different trust domain — default `http://localhost:8080` (yorkie.service.ts:41-42, plaintext), and in a real deployment a separate host or a managed Yorkie — and lands in that server's request handling/logs and in its auth-webhook cache key.

Attack: anyone who obtains one such token (Yorkie access/debug logs, an unencrypted backend↔Yorkie hop, a compromised or multi-tenant Yorkie project, a heap/config dump of the Yorkie side) plugs it into their own `yorkie.Client({ apiKey, authTokenInjector })` — the public API key already ships in every visitor's frontend bundle, as yorkie-auth.controller.ts:96-105 notes — and attaches to `sheet-<any id>` / `doc-<any id>` with verb `rw`. The webhook allows it unconditionally. There is no revocation short of rotating `JWT_SECRET`, which invalidates every session in the deployment, and nothing distinguishes the replay from the backend's own traffic.

The narrowing is cheap and available at the call site: `withDocument` knows the exact doc key it is about to attach, so `signYorkieServiceToken(secret, expiresIn, docKey)` plus an `attr.key === payload.docKey` check in `decide()` would reduce a leaked token from a project-wide master key to one document for 10 minutes. Restricting it to the methods the backend actually issues (ActivateClient/AttachDocument/PushPull/DetachDocument — never `GetRevision`) is the same one-line shape.

samples.summary: An allowed service token produces no log line, so use of a leaked service credential is invisible: the webhook has an audit trail only for denials
samples.evidence: `decide()` returns the shared `ALLOW` constant for the service identity (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215-217) and `handleAuth` logs only in the shadow-deny branch (lines 168-183). Nothing records that a project-wide credential was presented, for which document, or how often — the one identity whose misuse would be catastrophic is the one that leaves no trace. Since the backend's own use is low-volume (v1 endpoints, copies, seeds), even a debug-level `service token allowed method=… target=…` line would make anomalous use detectable. I grepped the controller and `Logger` uses in packages/backend/src/document and packages/backend/src/yorkie for any logging on the allow path and found none.

samples.summary: The master service token's lifetime is controlled by `YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN`, the same knob that sets end-user Yorkie token lifetime — lengthening one silently lengthens the other
samples.evidence: yorkie.service.ts:52-54 reads `YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN` (default 10m), the same variable `AuthService` uses for user/share tokens (auth.service.ts:68-70). An operator who lengthens user tokens to reduce `/auth/yorkie-token` chatter (a documented, innocuous-looking tuning) also lengthens the exposure window of a credential that grants read+write to every document, with no revocation. The service token is minted fresh per attach and only needs to outlive a single RPC round-trip, so it should carry its own short constant rather than inherit a user-facing knob.

samples.summary: The public-tier enforcement gate is now expressed twice with two different literals — `config.get(...) !== 'true'` in the seed command and `assertYorkieAuthEnforced` in the service — so the two can drift apart
samples.evidence: register-templates.ts previously called the shared helper; the delta replaces it with an inline `config.get<string>('YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE') !== 'true'` while template-review.ts:`assertYorkieAuthEnforced` keeps `enforce === 'true'`. They agree today only by coincidence of the literal. A later relaxation of the shared helper (e.g. accepting `'1'` or trimming whitespace) leaves the CLI stricter, and a later tightening leaves the CLI looser — a security gate whose semantics are duplicated rather than imported. Importing `assertYorkieAuthEnforced` (or a shared predicate) keeps the one definition the comment claims it mirrors.

verdict.reason: Verified directly in the repository; every element of the claim checks out. decide() returns the shared ALLOW constant for any token whose typ is 'yorkie-service' at yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215-217, placed before the CLIENT_METHODS check (line 220), the fail-closed empty-attributes check (line 228), the doc-key parse and verb check in checkAttribute (lines 251-257), and the REVISION_READ_METHODS elevation (line 83, applied at 257). The payload is signed as { typ: 'yorkie-service' } and nothing else (yorkie-service-token.ts:42), explicitly documented as carrying no subject (line 29), so it is bound to no document, method, verb or client - effectively read+write plus full revision history on every document in the project. The DocumentScopedIdentity union (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:49-52) structurally excludes the service type from hasAccess, confirming by construction that no per-document check can apply to it. The justification for accepting that blast radius - the claim that the token 'never leaves the process' at yorkie-auth.controller.ts:212, yorkie-service-token.ts:23 and docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:131 - is contradicted by the code: yorkie.service.ts:55-56 wraps signYorkieServiceToken in authTokenInjector, which is handed to the Yorkie SDK client at yorkie.service.ts:74, whose whole purpose is for the SDK to send the token to YORKIE_RPC_ADDR (default plaintext localhost:8080, lines 40-42) on every RPC issued in withDocument (lines 79-100); Yorkie then echoes it back in the webhook body, as auth.service.ts:33-34 itself describes. The credential therefore crosses a process and trust boundary and lands in that server's request handling, logs and auth-webhook cache key, and any replay of it is accepted unconditionally via auth.service.ts:95-106. Revocation is limited to rotating JWT_SECRET, the same secret backing every session (auth.service.ts:97); the 10-minute default expiry (yorkie.service.ts:52-54) bounds but does not remove the window. No refutation ground applies: the code is present exactly as described, no guard anywhere scopes the service identity (the type union proves the opposite), and unscoped authorization combined with sensitive-credential exposure is squarely in the security lane at the reviewer's 'major' tier - a clear weakness short of a full exploit, since it is gated on a token leak. The proposed narrowing is also demonstrably feasible: withDocument computes the exact doc key at yorkie.service.ts:70 and 76 before constructing the client at line 71, so it could pass it into the signer.

finding.summary: Public-template-tier precondition flipped from "requires explicit affirmation" to "passes by default", so the gate no longer detects the configuration it exists to refuse
finding.evidence:
Before this change `assertYorkieAuthEnforced` threw unless the operator had explicitly set `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE=true`. It now delegates to `isYorkieAuthEnforced` (packages/backend/src/yorkie/yorkie-auth-enforcement.ts:21 — `raw?.trim().toLowerCase() !== 'false'`), so `undefined` returns true and the gate passes on every stock deployment. The same inversion is applied to the seed script at packages/backend/src/template/seed/register-templates.ts:156.

The hazard the gate documents (template-review.ts:63-77) is unchanged: publishing publicly hands `previewToken` to every visitor, and a preview token is enough to *write* to the underlying Yorkie document unless `hasAccess()` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:240-273) actually runs. But `hasAccess()` only runs if the auth-webhook methods are registered on the Yorkie project — an out-of-band `yorkie project update --auth-webhook-method-add …` step the change itself acknowledges is separate (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:102-105, docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:26-30). On a deployment that never registered them (the stock state — there is no default registration anywhere in the repo; the only registration is documented shell commands in packages/backend/README.md:210 and packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:572), Yorkie never calls this endpoint at all, so the tier's precondition is unmet and yet `submit`/`approve` now succeed.

Attack: operator on a stock deployment publishes templates → gallery opens because the env gate is default-pass → an anonymous visitor takes `previewToken` from `/t/:id`, derives the Yorkie doc key from the returned `documentId`, attaches with the project public key that ships in the frontend bundle, and pushes writes to every public template document; each edit also returns the listing to review, draining the gallery into a reviewer-only queue (the second consequence template-review.ts:71-73 calls the deciding one). Previously the explicit `=true` was at least an operator affirmation

verdict.reason: The claimed inversion does not exist in this repository. `assertYorkieAuthEnforced` (template-review.ts:89-97) returns only for the literal string 'true' and throws BadRequestException for everything else, including `undefined`; it never imports or delegates to `isYorkieAuthEnforced` (the only consumer of that helper is yorkie-auth.controller.ts:9,133-134). The seed script applies the same strict literal check (`!== 'true'` → throw, register-templates.ts:157-161), not the alleged inversion. template.service.ts:468-475 feeds the raw env value into the strict gate at both submit and approve, and template-review.spec.ts:55-62 pins that undefined/''/'false'/'TRUE'/'1'/'yes' all throw. Because an unset YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE fails closed, the described attack chain (gallery opening by default on a stock deployment) has no entry point.
